metadata.title: Two maps of Congress: less divided in whom they name
metadata.author: Anas Mir, Martin Møllenhus, Diego A. Mijares

slides.title: They vote in two camps. Do they name in two?
bullets: Same 450 House members (2025-26) drawn twice: \textbf{working} = A cosponsors B's bill (46,513 ties); \textbf{floor} = A names B in a speech (17,824 speeches)
Floor: \textcolor{blue}{38.7%} of ties cross the aisle; working, cut to the same 3,970 ties: \textbf{28.6%} (mean of 200 draws, none close)
Party modularity 0.112 (floor) vs 0.211 (working); closest working partnerships cross only 12.8%
Both far more divided than chance: random rewiring gives about 50% cross-party
Checked: name matcher right in 98 of 100 hand-read mentions; holds with or without procedural yields

slides.title: You'd expect attacks. Mostly it's credit
bullets: We read 100 random floor mentions and coded each by hand (two coders agree 82%, kappa 0.64)
"I also thank my friend and subcommittee ranking member, Mr. Ro Khanna, for his collaboration this year" (Bacon, R)
Shuffling who is named \textbf{within each debate} drops modularity 0.112 to 0.074: procedure explains about two thirds
Louvain: working map splits into the \textbf{2 parties} (NMI 0.83); floor map into \textbf{8 bipartisan committee groups} (NMI 0.03)
A text classifier did not beat the baseline, so only hand codes are reported

items.sublabel: of cross-party mentions are thanks and credit
of floor division comes from how debates are run
of floor ties join committee colleagues (17% at random)

slides.title: At home, close seats name across the aisle
bullets: 55,023 press releases, 406 members. Exposed = district leans to own party by 5 points or less
Exposed vs safe: \textcolor{red}{13.3%} vs 9.2% (Republicans), \textcolor{blue}{11.6%} vs 9.0% (Democrats), p = 0.004 each; closest seats about 1 in 5
Exposed members are 22% of members but take part in about 1/3 of cross-party ties; 46 of 60 names read are partners or praise
Caveat: exposed members are also their party's moderates; seat and moderation cannot be separated
\textbf{How divided Congress looks depends on the record you read. A name, unlike "bipartisan", can be checked}
